sections.title: Network Security Baselines
sections.content:
SECURE BASELINES AND BENCHMARKS
Secure baseline — collection of standard configs/settings for network devices, software, patching, access controls, logging, monitoring, password policies, encryption, endpoint protection, etc. Improves manageability and operational consistency.
Resource | Description
CIS Benchmarks | Center for Internet Security best-practice guides; cover networks, OSes, applications; product-focused (Windows, macOS, Linux, Cisco, browsers, VMware ESXi) and framework-focused (PCI DSS, NIST 800-53, SOX, ISO 27000)
STIGs (Security Technical Implementation Guides) | DISA-developed baselines for US DoD IT infrastructure
Baseline management/compliance tools:
Tool | Purpose
Puppet, Chef, Ansible, Group Policy | Automate deployment of secure baseline configs, enforce consistency, detect/correct deviations
SCAP-compliant tools (OpenSCAP) | Assess/verify system adherence to baseline
CIS-CAT Pro | Assesses configs against CIS benchmarks
SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) | DISA tool measuring STIG compliance
HARDENING CONCEPTS
Default configs balance ease of use with security — well-documented credentials, simple passwords, and insecure protocols make defaults an attractive attack target. Hardening = changing defaults, often per published secure baselines.
Switch/Router hardening:
Action | Purpose
Change default credentials | Removes well-documented default access
Disable unnecessary services/interfaces | Reduces attack surface (avoid HTTP/Telnet)
Use secure management protocols | SSH instead of Telnet, HTTPS instead of HTTP
Implement ACLs | Restrict access to required devices/networks
Enable logging/monitoring | Detect login failures, config changes
Configure port security | Limits which devices can connect to a switch port
Strong password policies | Reduces password attack risk
Physically secure equipment | Locked rooms prevent physical tampering
Server hardening (adds to the above):
Action | Purpose
Apply patches/updates regularly | Fixes known vulnerabilities; automate for consistency
Least privilege principle | Limits impact of a compromised account
Firewalls and IDS | Block/alert on malicious activity
Secure configuration baselines | CIS or STIGs
Strong access controls | Password policy, MFA, PAM
Antivirus/antimalware | Detect and quarantine malware
Physical security | Racks, server rooms, datacenters
WIRELESS NETWORK INSTALLATION
Concept | Definition
BSSID | WAP's MAC address (identifies the access point)
SSID | Wireless network's name
Site Survey | Measures signal strength/channel usage across a site using architectural map + interference sources (walls, motors, microwaves)
Heat Map | Visual output of a site survey — shows signal strength (red=strong) and channel overlap
• 5 GHz band has more room for nonoverlapping channels than 2.4 GHz
• Bonded channels improve bandwidth but raise interference risk
• Heat map data drives adjustments: transmit power, channel changes, new/relocated WAPs
• Patchy coverage increases vulnerability to rogue APs and evil twin attacks
WIRELESS ENCRYPTION STANDARDS
Standard | Cipher | Key Notes
WEP | RC4 | Legacy, insecure
WPA v1 | RC4 + TKIP | Fixed some WEP flaws, still weak
WPA2 | AES + CCMP | CCMP provides authenticated encryption, replaces TKIP
WPA3 | AES + GCMP | Current standard; Enterprise mode requires 192-bit AES
WPA3 key features:
• SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — replaces PSK exchange, resists offline password capture
• Enhanced Open — encrypts traffic on open networks even without a password
• AES-GCMP — replaces AES-CCMP
• Wi-Fi Easy Connect — QR code-based device onboarding
Wi-Fi generation naming: 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6, 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5, 802.11n = Wi-Fi 4.
WPS AND EASY CONNECT
Method | Risk/Benefit
WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) | Push-button/PIN pairing; PIN splits into two brute-forceable halves (hours to crack); some devices can't fully disable it
Easy Connect (DPP) | WPA3-era replacement using QR codes/NFC + public/private key pairs; good for headless IoT provisioning
WI-FI AUTHENTICATION METHODS
Mode | Mechanism
WPA2-PSK (Personal) | Passphrase (8–63 ASCII chars) → PBKDF2 → 256-bit Pairwise Master Key (PMK); used in WPA2's 4-way handshake; min. 14-char passphrase recommended
WPA3-SAE (Personal) | Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) using the Dragonfly handshake (Diffie-Hellman over elliptic curves + MAC-derived hash); resists offline dictionary/brute force; provides forward secrecy
WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise | 802.1x port-based access control + RADIUS server; unique per-user credentials instead of shared passphrase; supports EAP-TLS (mutual cert auth), EAP-TTLS/PEAP (server-cert tunnel)
Note: WPA3-Personal Transition mode (legacy WPA2 support) has been shown vulnerable to downgrade attacks.
RADIUS AUTHENTICATION WORKFLOW
• Supplicant (user device) connects to the NAS (access point/switch/VPN gateway)
• NAS prompts for credentials (RADIUS supports PAP, CHAP, EAP — EAP is standard now)
• Supplicant sends EAPoL data; RADIUS client builds an encrypted Access-Request packet (UDP port 1812)
• AAA server decrypts using the shared secret (no response if it fails)
• Access-Challenge/Access-Request exchange occurs for EAP setup
• Server responds Access-Accept or Access-Reject
Accounting (logging) uses UDP port 1813 and can run on a separate server.
NETWORK ACCESS CONTROL (NAC)
Authenticates users/devices AND checks/enforces security policy compliance (OS version, patch level, AV status) before granting network access.
• Dynamic VLAN assignment — NAC assigns a VLAN based on identity, device type, location, or health check results (e.g., vendor → Internet-only VLAN)
• Quarantine VLAN — noncompliant devices (e.g., outdated AV) automatically isolated
NAC Approach | Description
Agent-Based | Software agent on the device reports status/compliance; enables automatic remediation
Agentless | Port-based NAC or network scans (e.g., DHCP fingerprinting); works with any device, less detailed info
• Persistent agent — installed as a software application
• Nonpersistent/dissolvable agent — loaded into memory during posture assessment only, not installed

sections.title: Network Security Capability Enhancement
sections.content:
ACCESS CONTROL LISTS VS. FIREWALL RULES
Concept | Scope
ACL | Rules on routers/switches controlling traffic at the interface level (source/dest IP, port, protocol)
Firewall Rule | Governs inbound/outbound traffic for IPs/ranges/interfaces; network + application-level control
• Rules process top-to-bottom; most specific rules go first
• Implicit deny — default rule blocking anything unmatched (add explicit deny-all if not automatic)
• Each rule specifies tuples: protocol, source address/port, destination address/port
Firewall configuration principles:
• Block incoming requests from spoofed internal/private IPs
• Block incoming local-only protocol traffic (ICMP, DHCP, routing protocols) at the perimeter
• Use pen testing to confirm configuration; log and monitor access attempts
• Secure the firewall hardware and its management interface
• Can restrict outbound traffic too (e.g., block outbound port 25/SMTP to stop spam from a compromised host)
SCREENED SUBNET (PERIMETER NETWORK / DMZ)
Creates a neutral zone separating public-facing servers (web, email, DNS, FTP) from the internal network.
• First firewall (Internet ↔ screened subnet) — allows traffic to hosted services
• Second firewall (screened subnet ↔ internal network) — blocks nearly all traffic inbound to internal network
• A core example of network segmentation as a security control
IDS AND IPS
System | Behavior
IDS (Intrusion Detection System) | Passive — monitors, alerts administrators; does not block traffic
IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) | Active — detects AND blocks/mitigates (drop packets, reset connections, block source)
Deployment | Strength | Limitation
HIDS/HIPS (host-based) | Insider threats, file integrity, non-network events (local logins) | Confined to the host it's installed on
NIDS/NIPS (network-based) | Cross-system threats (DDoS, network scanning) | No host-specific visibility
Notable tools:
Tool | Role
Snort | Rule-driven IDS; combines signature, protocol, anomaly-based inspection; large community ruleset
Suricata | High-performance IDS/IPS/NSM; Snort-rule compatible; can run as IDS or IPS
Security Onion | Linux distro bundling Snort, Suricata, and other network security monitoring tools
OSSEC | Open-source HIDS — log analysis, integrity checking, registry monitoring, rootkit detection
DETECTION METHODS
Method | Mechanism
Signature-Based | Matches traffic against a database of known attack patterns; requires regular signature/plug-in/feed updates
Behavioral/Anomaly-Based | Trained on baseline "normal" traffic; flags deviations; can catch zero-days and insider threats, but generates false positives/negatives while learning
Machine-learning behavior-detection classes (per Gartner):
Class | Scope
UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) | Scans multiple IDS/log sources; often integrated with SIEM
NTA (Network Traffic Analysis) | Applies analysis only to network streams, similar to NBAD
• Anomaly-based detection can also mean strict RFC/protocol-compliance checking, not just behavioral learning
• Trend analysis — tracking events/alerts over time to spot growing threats, tune out false positives, and guide security investment
WEB FILTERING
Deployment Model | Description
Agent-Based | Software agent on each device enforces policy via cloud management server; works off-network (remote/travel); detailed per-device reporting
Centralized Proxy | Intermediary between users and Internet; controls/monitors all web traffic; supports caching and anonymizing requests
Centralized proxy filtering techniques:
Technique | Function
URL Scanning | Blocks specific known-malicious/inappropriate URLs
Content Categorization | Classifies sites (social media, gambling, adult, webmail) for policy-based blocking
Block Rules | Blocks by URL/domain/IP/category/keyword (e.g., all .exe downloads)
Reputation-Based Filtering | Scores sites by observed behavior/history; auto-blocks poor-reputation sites
Web filtering issues:
• Overblocking — too restrictive, blocks legitimate sites, hurts productivity
• Underblocking — too permissive, allows harmful content through
• Encrypted traffic (HTTPS) — filters may be unable to inspect without proper config; decrypting/inspecting HTTPS raises employee privacy concerns

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Select a secure baseline based on careful analysis of the organization's risk profile
• Automate the rollout and management of secure baselines using tools such as Active Directory Group Policy, Ansible, Puppet, or Chef
• Continuously audit wireless networks to ensure proper configuration and validate access points
• Implement enterprise network authentication methods to enrich logging, improve data protection, and provide granular control
• Enforce network security requirements through the implementation of NAC "gate-keepers"
• Use firewalls, IDS/IPS, and web filtering to monitor and control network traffic and block access to malicious or inappropriate content

practice_questions.q: A documented set of approved, secure settings applied to every new server is called a:
practice_questions.explanation: Baselines define the secure starting configuration.

practice_questions.q: A firewall rule allows SSH from anywhere. The team changes it to allow SSH only from the admin subnet. What capability is being modified?
Which wireless setup gives each user individual credentials checked against a RADIUS server?
practice_questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually.

practice_questions.q: Which email security record lists the mail servers allowed to send mail for a domain?
practice_questions.explanation: Sender Policy Framework lists authorized senders.

practice_questions.q: A company lets employees use personal phones for work but manages a separate work container on them. What deployment model is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Bring your own device uses personally owned phones.

practice_questions.q: Which email technology adds a digital signature to messages so receivers can verify they were not altered?
practice_questions.explanation: DomainKeys Identified Mail signs outgoing mail.

practice_questions.q: The company buys phones, owns them, but lets employees use them personally too. What model is this?
Which email record tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails SPF or DKIM checks?
practice_questions.explanation: DMARC sets the policy (none, quarantine, reject) and reporting.

practice_questions.q: Which tool lets IT push policies, require a PIN and remotely wipe lost company phones?
practice_questions.explanation: MDM manages and secures mobile devices.

practice_questions.q: The company blocks access to known malicious domains by refusing to resolve them. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: DNS filtering stops lookups of bad domains.
